summary:
The legal framework a trans visitor meets in Colombia is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition, without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025. Courts have also intervened directly in detention, ruling on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty and protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

The gap between that framework and enforcement is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025 alone. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.

No department-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding was located for Nariño; the 2025 national reporting flags it neither for a public-order regime nor for territorial expansion of anti-LGBTIQ+ violence. It otherwise inherits national conditions, and the national homicide figures used in that reporting cover Nariño: 41 trans people killed in 2023, 8 killed between February and April 2024, 13 killed in the first quarter of 2025, alongside the 35 LGBTI murders recorded by the Attorney General's Office between January and May 2025.

The sharpest risk sits where armed groups operate. Reporting on threats and displacement by armed groups is treated as national in scope and covers Nariño, even though the specific incidents documented occurred elsewhere. In the department of Caquetá, armed groups ran "social cleansing" campaigns announced through flyers distributed on the street and via WhatsApp naming "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets, a campaign by armed groups still operating despite the 2016 peace agreement. In the department of Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans".

Targeted killings of trans people also continue in ordinary urban settings. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín in April 2025; a video of the assault went viral from 5 April, and she died the following afternoon. Police interrogated local residents but no one had been arrested as of the April 2025 reporting. President Gustavo Petro asked authorities to investigate urgently, and events were held in several cities to denounce transphobia.

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.
tangentialFactors:
Discrimination against trans women in Colombia confines most of them to hairdressing or sex work, which shapes exposure to street violence and to armed-group threats. In Caquetá, three armed men gave trans woman Tatiana Cespedes, 51, one week to leave town or be killed; after hiding for a week she fled at night.

The pattern of fatal attacks extends beyond headline cases. Reporting from April 2025 recalls earlier killings: gay men lured through an app and killed, a trans rough-sleeper stabbed while sleeping, and others killed in their homes or in a hairdresser. One report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025.

Graeme Reid's May 2025 assessment sets Colombia's reforms against a rising toll of killings, treating the disconnect between legislation and daily lived experience as the central problem rather than a gap in the law itself. The prosecution of conflict-era anti-LGBT violence as gender persecution by the Special Jurisdiction for Peace is an unusual international-law route; most killings are handled as ordinary homicide, and arrests in individual cases have been slow.

The official Reyes, who defended the change, described the previous judicial examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 underpins recognition on the basis of self-recognition without any surgical requirement.

Identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015. Residents deprived of liberty have direct judicial protection: a Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman in custody and on the rights of trans detainees in the prison system. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging gender persecution as a crime against humanity.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Nariño-specific source in this inventory addresses municipal ordinances, police practice, restroom or facility access, healthcare provision, or hate-crime prosecutions within the department. Those points are unresolved rather than absent.

The sources give national killing totals that are stated to cover Nariño, but no count of trans or LGBTI homicides recorded in Nariño itself. Whether armed groups with a presence elsewhere in Colombia operate in Nariño is not established here; the armed-group threats and displacement described come from Caquetá and Guajira.

Whether the comprehensive trans law under consideration in 2025 was enacted is unresolved. In the Sara Millerey case, the April 2025 reporting states that police interrogated local residents and that no arrest had been made; the current status of that investigation is not sourced.
